title: The Limit of a Function
lead: A limit describes how a function behaves near a number rather than at it. Here limits are estimated from tables of functional values and from graphs, taken from the left and from the right, and extended to functions that grow without bound near a number, where the graph has a vertical asymptote.
objectives: Using correct notation, describe the limit of a function.
Use a table of values to estimate the limit of a function or to identify when the limit does not exist.
Use a graph to estimate the limit of a function or to identify when the limit does not exist.
Define one-sided limits and provide examples.
Explain the relationship between one-sided and two-sided limits.
Using correct notation, describe an infinite limit.
summary_html:
• A table of values or graph may be used to estimate a limit.
  • If the limit of a function at a point does not exist, it is still possible that the limits from the left and right at that point may exist.
  • If the limits of a function from the left and right exist and are equal, then the limit of the function is that common value.
  • We may use limits to describe infinite behavior of a function at a point.

exercises.prompt:
Evaluate each of the following limits, if possible. Use a table of functional values and graph $f(x)=1/x^{2}$ to confirm your conclusion.

a. $\lim_{x\to 0^{-}}\frac{1}{x^{2}}$

b. $\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}\frac{1}{x^{2}}$

c. $\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x^{2}}$

answer.solution: a. $\lim_{x\to 0^{-}}\frac{1}{x^{2}}=+\infty;$ b. $\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}\frac{1}{x^{2}}=+\infty;$ c. $\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x^{2}}=+\infty$ Hint: Follow the procedures from Example 2.9.

exercises.prompt:
Evaluate each of the following limits. Identify any vertical asymptotes of the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}.$

a. $\lim_{x\to 2^{-}}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}$

b. $\lim_{x\to 2^{+}}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}$

c. $\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}$

answer.solution: a. $\lim_{x\to 2^{-}}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}=-\infty;$ b. $\lim_{x\to 2^{+}}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}=+\infty;$ c. $\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}$ DNE. The line $x=2$ is the vertical asymptote of $f(x)=1/(x-2)^{3}.$ Hint: Use Infinite Limits from Positive Integers.

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, consider the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ shown here. Which of the statements about $y=f(x)$ are true and which are false? Explain why a statement is false.

$\lim_{x\to 10}f(x)=0$

answer.solution: True. Near $x=10$ the graph is its last segment, a smooth curve that crosses the $x$-axis at $(10,0)$ with no hole and no break, so as $x$ approaches 10 from either side the values $f(x)$ approach 0, and $\lim_{x\to 10}f(x)=0.$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, consider the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ shown here. Which of the statements about $y=f(x)$ are true and which are false? Explain why a statement is false.

$\lim_{x\to -8}f(x)=f(-8)$

answer.solution: False. The vertex of the first segment, $(-8,-6),$ is an open circle, and the closed circle at $(-8,-3)$ gives the value of the function, so $f(-8)=-3.$ As $x$ approaches $-8$ from either side, the values $f(x)$ approach $-6,$ so $\lim_{x\to -8}f(x)=-6\ne -3=f(-8).$

figure.alt: A graph in quadrant one of the density of a shock wave against distance x: the level ρ₁ from 0 to x_SF, a vertical drop at x_SF from ρ₁ to ρ₂, and the level ρ₂ for x ≥ x_SF, with ρ₁ > ρ₂.

exercises.prompt:
Shock waves arise in many physical applications, ranging from supernovas to detonation waves. A graph of the density of a shock wave with respect to distance, x, is shown here. We are mainly interested in the location of the front of the shock, labeled $x_{\text{SF}}$ in the diagram.

a. Evaluate $\lim_{x\to x_{\text{SF}}^{+}}\rho(x).$

b. Evaluate $\lim_{x\to x_{\text{SF}}^{-}}\rho(x).$

c. Evaluate $\lim_{x\to x_{\text{SF}}}\rho(x).$ Explain the physical meanings behind your answers.

answer.solution: a. $\rho_{2}$ b. $\rho_{1}$ c. DNE unless $\rho_{1}=\rho_{2}.$ As you approach $x_{\text{SF}}$ from the left, you are in the high-density area of the shock. When you approach from the right, you have not experienced the “shock” yet and are at a lower density.
